3|Early Surgery for Asymptomatic Aortic Stenosis
4|Trial Procedures
5|Eligibility was determined after each patient un-
6|derwent a thorough evaluation of symptoms and
7|medical records and results of echocardiography
8|and exercise testing were reviewed. Details re-
9|garding echocardiography and exercise testing are
10|provided in the Supplementary Appendix, available
11|at NEJM.org. Patients were randomly assigned in
12|a 1:1 ratio to early surgery or conservative care
13|with the use of a Web-based interactive response
14|system. The assignment to each treatment group
15|was computer-generated and stratified according
16|to the participating center by means of a permuted-
17|block sequence with variable block size.
18|The protocol specified that patients assigned
19|to the early-surgery group should undergo aortic-
20|valve replacement within 2 months after random-
21|ization. Patients assigned to the conservative-care
22|group received treatment according to the ACC-
23|AHA guidelines,2,12 and they were referred for
24|surgery if they became symptomatic during fol-
25|low-up, if the left ventricular ejection fraction
26|decreased to less than 50%, or if the peak aortic
27|jet velocity increased each year by more than 0.5 m
28|per second on follow-up echocardiography. Details
29|regarding surgical procedures and patient follow-
30|up are provided in the Supplementary Appendix.
31|Trial End Points
32|The primary end point was a composite of op-
33|erative mortality or death from cardiovascular
34|causes during the follow-up period (continuing
35|until 4 years after the last patient was enrolled).
36|Prespecified secondary end points included death
37|from any cause, repeat aortic-valve surgery, clini-
38|cal thromboembolic events, and hospitalization
39|for heart failure during follow-up. Specific defi-
40|nitions of trial end points are provided in the
41|Supplementary Appendix.
42|Statistical Analysis
43|On the basis of our previous observational study,13
44|we estimated that a sample of 144 patients would
45|provide the trial with 80% power, at a two-sided
46|significance level of 0.05, to detect a significant
47|difference with respect to the primary end point,
48|assuming that the incidence of the primary end
49|point would be 16% in the conservative-care group
50|and 2% in the early-surgery group during a follow-
51|up period that continued until 4 years after the last
52|patient was enrolled. In calculating the sample size
53|by a log-rank survival power analysis, we also
54|assumed that an enrollment period of 2 years
55|would be needed to complete enrollment and that
56|the rate of loss to follow-up would be 10%.
57|Analyses were performed on an intention-to-
58|treat basis. Differences between the treatment
59|groups were evaluated with the use of Student's
60|t-test for continuous variables and Fisher's exact
61|test for categorical variables. Because random-
62|ization was stratified according to the partici-
63|pating center, we analyzed the end points with
64|the use of stratified Cox proportional-hazards re-
65|gression with Firth correction. Estimates of cu-
66|mulative incidences were calculated by the Kaplan-
67|Meier method and were compared with the use
68|of the log-rank test. For the Kaplan-Meier analy-
69|sis, we analyzed all clinical events according to
70|the time to the first event. Hazard ratios with
71|95% confidence intervals were derived with the
72|use of the stratified Cox proportional-hazards
73|model with Firth correction. The 95% confidence
74|intervals have not been adjusted for multiple com-
75|parisons, and therefore inferences drawn from
76|these intervals may not be reproducible.
77|For the primary end-point analysis, we also
78|performed a competing-risk analysis in which
79|death due to a cause other than a cardiovascular
80|cause was considered as a competing risk, and
81|hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals were
82|calculated with the use of the method of Fine and
83|Gray. The cumulative incidences of the primary
84|end point were also compared between the treat-
85|ment groups with the use of Gray's test. Subgroup
86|analyses were performed to determine whether
87|the result of the primary end point was consistent
88|in two prespecified subgroups defined according
89|to peak aortic velocity and cause of aortic stenosis.
90|A per-protocol analysis of the primary end point
91|was also performed. All reported P values were
92|two-sided, and a P value of less than 0.05 was
93|considered to indicate statistical significance. We
94|used SAS software, version 9.4 (SAS Institute), for
95|statistical analyses.

eh_4a4db61b21438e7b.quote:
Statistical Analysis Plan

Sample Size Calculation
We tried to determine the rate of primary endpoint based on the randomized trials, but no randomized
trial has been conducted to evaluate outcomes of early surgery. Using a prospective registry data, we
recently reported that the estimated actuarial 6-year survival and cardiac mortality-free survival rates
were 98±1% and 100% in the early surgery group, 68±6% and 76±5% in the conventional treatment
group, respectively (p < 0.001) (9). Based on our prospective observational study, we estimated that a
sample size of 144 patients would provide 80% power to detect a significant difference with respect to
the primary end point at the 2-sided significance level of 0.05, assuming that the 4-year rate of a
composite end point (cardiac mortality or operative mortality) would be 16% in the conventional
treatment group and 2% in the early surgery group.

Analysis of primary and secondary end point
All primary and secondary endpoints will be analyzed on an intent-to-treat basis (all patients analyzed
as part of their assigned treatment group). For intent-to-treat analysis, all patients who sign the written
informed consent form and are randomized in the study will be included in the analysis, regardless of
whether or not the correct treatment is administered, or whether crossover occurs.
To analyze outcomes, estimates of cumulative event rates will be calculated by the Kaplan-Meier
method and compared employing the log-rank test. For Kaplan-Meier analysis, we will analyze all
clinical events by time to first event. Hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals will be derived with
the use of the Cox proportional hazards model.
Subgroup analyses will be performed to determine whether the reduction in the primary end point after
early surgery is consistent in 2 prespecified subgroups of peak aortic velocity (<5 m/s vs. ≥5 m/s) and
etiology of AS (degenerative vs. non-degenerative), using Cox regression models with tests for
interaction.

eh_fb45d1def9f691b8.quote:
4. Study Endpoint

4.1 Primary Endpoint
A composite of operative mortality or cardiovascular mortalities that occur during entire follow-up (a
minimum of 4 years)

Operative mortality is defined as death within 30 days of AV surgery.
Cardiovascular mortality is defined as sudden cardiac death, death from myocardial infarction, heart
failure, complications of cardiac surgery or intervention, cerebrovascular disease or other
cardiovascular disease.
Sudden cardiac death is defined as either witnessed instantaneous unexpected death or unwitnessed
unexpected death, if other cause of death was excluded with reasonable certainty.

4.2 Secondary Endpoint

 All-cause death occurring during entire follow-up (a minimum of 4 years)
 Repeat AV surgery occurring during entire follow-up (a minimum of 4 years)
 Clinical thromboembolic events during entire follow-up (a minimum of 4 years)
 Hospitalization due to congestive heart failure during entire follow-up (a minimum of 4
years)

checkpoint_answers.justification: The captured protocol identifies the trial and is dated 1 February 2010; its contents state that it includes the original SAP as the only version. That plan specifies the primary composite and ITT analysis, Kaplan–Meier/log-rank methods, and Cox hazard ratios. The protocol’s July 2014 revision summary concerns study timeline and exercise-testing eligibility, not analysis; recruitment began July 2010. The report presents the matching primary composite/ITT result and says the authors vouch for fidelity to protocol. This supports, by inference, a prespecified applicable plan before unblinded data were available. However, the approved HR is reported as Fine–Gray, a method not listed in the SAP, and the captured sources do not date investigators’ access to unblinded outcomes; thus not a definitive yes.
unknowns: When investigators first had access to unblinded outcome data.
Whether the Fine–Gray primary HR method was specified outside the captured original SAP.

counterevidence.implication: The SAP specifies Cox HRs, while the article identifies the reported primary HR as Fine–Gray; this leaves a method correspondence gap, although the article also reports Cox analyses and does not explain the choice as result-driven.

limitations.premise: The captured protocol/SAP does not establish when investigators accessed unblinded results, and it does not show whether the reported Fine–Gray HR was prespecified elsewhere.
limitations.stopping_rationale: Inspected the full protocol chronology, change summary, original SAP, and main-report analysis/result passages; registry retrieval is unavailable at normal intake. The support for early prespecification is therefore inferential, not conclusive.

checkpoint_answers.justification: The protocol specifies one primary composite endpoint—operative mortality or cardiovascular mortality over the entire follow-up (minimum four years)—with its component definitions. The approved result is that same composite and follow-up target, and the report presents the primary endpoint result plus cumulative-incidence information at follow-up times; the inspected sources do not indicate that one among multiple eligible primary-domain measurements was selectively fully reported because of its result. Other specified secondary endpoints are distinct outcomes, not alternative measurements of this primary composite.

The SAP specifies ITT, Kaplan–Meier/log-rank and Cox HR analyses. The report describes stratified Cox with Firth correction, Kaplan–Meier/Gray, a Fine–Gray competing-risk analysis for the primary endpoint, and per-protocol/subgroup analyses; its primary HR is specifically attributed to Fine–Gray. Thus multiple analyses are possible and at least some method detail differs from the SAP. Neither the captured report nor protocol establishes that the reported estimate was chosen because it was favorable or that competing analyses were withheld for their results. Multiplicity/mismatch alone cannot support probable selection; the basis for any choice remains unresolved.
unknowns: Whether the Fine–Gray analysis and other reported analyses were prespecified or supplementary, and whether analyses/results were withheld because of their findings.

counterevidence.implication: The plan/report method difference and several reported methods establish multiplicity or possible deviation, but do not establish result-driven selection; the report provides more than one primary-endpoint analysis/result summary.

limitations.premise: The captured Sources do not explain why the Fine–Gray estimate was used for the reported primary HR or establish whether eligible alternative analyses were withheld based on results.
limitations.stopping_rationale: Inspected the original SAP, the final-protocol analysis passage, the protocol change summary, and main-report statistical methods and primary-endpoint results. The registry is unavailable at intake; remaining result-dependence cannot be resolved from these captured passages.
